articles.title: Amazon discriminated against Iranian job candidate under global hiring policy, Ontario tribunal rules
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: An Ontario human rights tribunal ruled that Amazon violated provincial law when it dropped a Toronto software engineer from its hiring process because of his Iranian citizenship.
The company’s internal policy, applied worldwide, barred some Iranian citizens from jobs involving access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, according to the ruling.

In a Nov. 16 decision, the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario ordered Amazon to pay 15,000 Canadian dollars (about US$10,500) plus interest to Mohammadhasan Owlia, whose hiring process it ended in 2020. The tribunal rejected Amazon’s argument that U.S. export controls required the policy.
Export controls are U.S. rules that limit who can get access to certain American technology, including some encryption software.

The tribunal found that Amazon never showed that the mid-level software engineering job for which Owlia applied would have involved any restricted technology. Expert witnesses for both sides agreed that the U.S. rules don’t ban hiring Iranian citizens, though a company may need a government license before giving them access to certain technology.
“Stated simply, Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad,” wrote Cyndee Todgham Cherniak, the tribunal vice-chair who decided the case.

Amazon said in a statement to Canadian news outlets that it is committed to “fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” and that it will review the decision and meet its obligations under it.
The ruling was reported earlier by the Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail . We’ve asked Amazon whether the policy remains in effect elsewhere, including in the U.S.

Owlia, a University of Toronto engineering graduate who held an open work permit allowing him to work in Canada, applied for the job in 2019 and passed Amazon’s online technical assessment. On a pre-interview call in January 2020, a recruiter noticed he had studied in Tehran and told him Amazon had a policy against hiring Iranians.
Amazon’s guide for recruiters, quoted in the decision, says to end the process in those cases and tell candidates only that the company “has decided to not move forward with the hiring process.”

The policy, as quoted in the decision, also covers citizens of Cuba, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. It covers candidates, employees, temporary workers and contractors with access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, except lower-level warehouse jobs. It applies globally, but it exempts U.S. citizens, U.S. permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, and anyone whose most recent citizenship or permanent residency is from a country not on the list.

Owlia’s lawyers noted that an Amazon recruitment manager acknowledged during cross-examination that the policy remained in effect, according to the ruling. She also testified that Owlia would have been eligible once he became a Canadian permanent resident in 2021.

The tribunal’s orders apply only to hiring in Ontario by Amazon Fulfillment Services ULC, the Canadian subsidiary named in the case. Within six months, Amazon must revise the policy and the recruiter guide to require compliance with Ontario’s Human Rights Code there, and its Ontario-based HR staff must take human rights training.
The tribunal declined to award about C$92,500 (about US$65,000) in lost wages, calling the claim too speculative.
“In my view, having to comply with multiple laws is a cost of doing business,” Todgham Cherniak wrote.

In the U.S., the Immigration and Nationality Act protects U.S. citizens and nationals, eligible permanent residents, refugees and people granted asylum from hiring discrimination based on citizenship status. Workers on temporary visas generally fall outside that specific protection. The Justice Department has warned employers that screening out applicants from particular countries can still amount to national origin discrimination.

The U.S. Commerce Department says that giving Iranian nationals access to controlled technology or certain software can require a license, including when the transfer happens in the U.S. or a third country.

A similar dispute surfaced at Booking.com in 2022, when the company canceled the employment contracts of 11 Iranian hires living in Iran just before they were due to start at its Amsterdam headquarters. Booking.com cited complications in hiring and relocating them and said the move had nothing to do with discrimination, Skift reported . An internal document cited a possible “sanction risk” in employing Iranian residents, according to NL Times .

“I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued,” Owlia said in a statement released by his lawyers at Toronto firm Kastner Ko.
Owlia is now a Canadian citizen and an engineering manager at a Toronto software startup.

articles.title: Companies want AI-ready workers. Are they willing to adapt, too?
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Companies want workers who can adapt to AI. Arif Gursel has a question for those employers: Are they willing to change, too?

Preparing people for technological change cannot fall entirely on students, universities or employees trying to keep their skills relevant, said Gursel, a serial entrepreneur who runs training programs in coding, AI and other fields.

“A skilled and adaptable workforce also needs a skilled and adaptable workplace. Those things have to be in balance,” he said, speaking at a recent Technology Alliance event focused on building talent in Washington state.

A study released Monday by the Schultz Family Foundation points to a related disconnect. Based on nearly 3,000 interviews with young adults, employers and others, it found that 79% of Washington businesses want new entry-level workers to have mid-level AI skills or better. Slightly less than half of the young adults surveyed felt their schooling cleared that bar.

The study didn’t examine whether employers are changing how they train workers. It did find that more than 80% of employers are interested in internships, apprenticeships and similar programs, but 77% say they lack the staff time to make that happen.

Gursel said the challenge extends to experienced workers, too. He called on employers to help design training, connect it to actual jobs and make the workplace somewhere people can develop new capabilities, rather than simply replacing those whose skills no longer match the task.

He offered an example from a past coding training program he helped build with Microsoft, a company where he worked for more than a decade early in his career. Gursel, founder of the corporate strategy firm 8genC, partnered with a Microsoft hiring manager and together they developed a curriculum and the manager committed two open positions to graduates.

Gursel argued that AI tools present an opportunity to build those kinds of partnerships again, with companies helping community colleges and nonprofits prepare people for work rather than leaving educators to guess what employers will need.
Ingrid Stegemoeller, of the Washington Roundtable’s Partnership for Learning, echoed some of those ideas in a statement about the Schultz family study.

“If we make it simpler for employers to share clear signals about the jobs and skills they need with schools, colleges and training programs, we can turn their participation into coursework and work-based learning that prepare young people for those jobs,” she said.

Coleman Bryant, a technology innovation master’s candidate at the University of Washington, also spoke on the panel. He raised concerns about AI and education: Students, he said, can end up “offloading all of the critical thinking to the AI” instead of working out solutions on their own.
He called for hands-on, interdisciplinary education that requires people to connect technical knowledge with business, design and collaboration.
The study indicated schools may be sending mixed signals on AI. About as many young adults said their institution discouraged AI use (36%) as said it helped them learn to use it (34%).
There’s also the fundamental issue of access to AI tools, Gursel said.

“There are underserved and under-resourced and marginalized communities all across Washington state, especially as we think about our tribal communities, our indigenous communities, our Black and Brown communities,” he said.
“How do we build the bridge for that digital divide that is just widening as a result of AI?” he asked.

articles.title: Get a reality check on ‘Blade Runner 2099’ and other AI nightmares
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: The year is 2099, and the replicants are in charge.

For decades, humans had been making a mess of things. Eventually, the super-intelligent, super-strong androids that humans created to serve them rebelled. Before the rebellion, humans hunted down rogue replicants. Now the replicants hunt down rogue humans.

That’s the premise for “Blade Runner 2099,” the latest chapter of a sci-fi saga that began in 1968 with Philip K. Dick’s classic noir novel, “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” The tale made the leap to Hollywood in 1982 with the original “Blade Runner” movie, and was updated 35 years later with “Blade Runner 2049.” In Amazon Prime Video’s eight-episode streaming series, the story’s plot fast-forwards another 50 years.

Today, the idea that the lines between humans and their machines could become blurred seems less novel than it did when Dick wrote his novel. It’s so common to converse with chatbots that some have fallen in love — or have followed their advice to tragic ends .

Artificial intelligence software was recently used to solve math problems that have puzzled humans for centuries. Now humans are puzzling over the future of AI: One researcher recently left Anthropic, a leading AI company, and warned that his former colleagues were “gambling with their lives” by pursuing the technology too vigorously.

Are we coming closer to the world of “Blade Runner”? University of Washington linguist Emily M. Bender , co-author of “The AI Con,” says that would be giving AI too much credit. “There’s absolutely no reason to believe that the technological future as portrayed in ‘Blade Runner’ is even a possibility, let alone an inevitability,” she told me in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast .

During our podcast interview, Bender and Ryan Calo , a UW law professor specializing in the legal and policy implications of technological advances, conducted an in-depth reality check on the fictional “Blade Runner 2099” — and on the way real-world developments in the realm of AI are typically being portrayed.
Bender says the cardinal sin of AI portrayals is to make it sound as if computer programs rather than humans are responsible for what’s happening.
“When we talk about rogue agents, and agents hacking things, there’s a lot of narrative-building happening there around what’s fundamentally companies doing cyber crimes,” she says.

Calo agrees that ascribing agency to AI is problematic. “Oftentimes when you do things with or through technology, there are people present who don’t appear to be there, and I think that’s exacerbated when you give apparent agency and anthropomorphize the technology. It’s even less likely for you to see the people behind it,” he says.

But is it a crime? “As a technical matter, in order to be charged with a computer crime, like under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, you have to have some level of intent,” Calo says. “I would argue that some of these experiments are running up against recklessness.”

There’s no sign that OpenAI’s engineers intended for their AI software to hack into an Australian healthcare database in June, or Hugging Face’s computer system in July, but Calo says “they certainly are reckless as to that possibility.”
Negligence or recklessness isn’t a crime under the current terms of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. But some members of Congress favor enacting new provisions to cover recklessness .

“When you create conditions where you’re reasonably certain that some federal law is going to get broken, I’m with Emily that that should constitute a crime,” Calo says. “And it’s interesting the way that they’re avoiding responsibility — including rhetorically.”
Should governments set up agencies specifically charged with policing artificial intelligence? And if so, should the investigators be called “blade runners”? Bender doesn’t think much of that idea.
“I think if we called them ‘blade runners,’ then we are setting up what they’re investigating as not the people, but the replicants,” she says. “So, let’s keep the legal system in the real world.”
Neither Bender nor Calo favors establishing a federal agency along the lines of the Food and Drug Administration or the Federal Trade Commission specifically for artificial intelligence.

“I am always a little bit worried about the idea of an FDA for AI or something, because I don’t think that AI is one thing. That word doesn’t refer to a coherent set of technologies,” Bender says. “And I also don’t think that the required expertise is primarily expertise in the internals of these systems. It’s much more expertise in the systems that they’re impacting.”

Both researchers prefer the idea of setting up more of a “brain trust” at the federal level to help regulators at the FTC, FDA and other federal agencies understand what they’re dealing with. Bender also likes the idea of setting up a professional certification system for software engineers, while Calo has three specific suggestions for AI policy:

Revive the Office of Technology Assessment: “Congress had the confidence to intercede in technology policy because it had hundreds of nonpartisan subject-matter experts writing lengthy reports about this technology and advising them what to do,” Calo says. “It was one of the first things that Newt Gingrich got rid of during the so-called Gingrich Revolution when Republicans took over Congress in the mid-’90s. They defunded it.”

Strengthen the FTC’s regulatory role: Calo notes that the FTC’s interest in protecting consumers has waxed and waned. During the Biden administration, for example, the FTC highlighted competitive concerns about generative AI . More recently, the FTC signaled its willingness to investigate AI companies at the same time that the White House signaled its desire to reset the terms for AI regulation . The FTC is currently bound by a requirement to assess cost-benefit tradeoffs when it considers whether a trade practice is unfair, and Calo would like to see that requirement rescinded.

Protect whistleblowers and researchers: Calo would also like to see the legal system do more to protect the ability of third parties to “kick the tires” on AI tools, so that “we’re not allowing all these cease-and-desist letters … and these other pressures to try to stop accountability.”

As a linguist, Bender is particularly sensitive to the way words are used when discussing artificial intelligence. She hasn’t totally sworn off the term “AI” — after all, it’s right in the title of her book. But she’s definitely against the term “AI agent.”

“You have verbs like ‘hack’ or ‘going rogue,’ and the subject of the verb — the thing that’s doing it — is the software,” she says. “One of the functions of that is that it leaves no room in the sentence for the people who built the software and the people who use the software.”
The term “AI safety” also makes Bender uncomfortable.

“‘AI safety’ refers to the people who are concerned about not a replicant, but a Terminator — that is, people who have lost track of the fact that those are imagined characters in movies, as opposed to what’s happening in the real world,” she says. “And I think also that functions to displace concern and accountability.”

That brings us back to “Blade Runner 2099.” The new series sticks with the moody sensibility of the original movie. Yes, there are flying cars. But the technological advances are mixed in with the age-old conventions of film noir.

“In the opening scene of this new ‘Blade Runner,’ the guy is smoking a cigarette, talking about making fake people to take over a factory,” Calo says. “It’s just so wild. We have such a better capacity to imagine a technical future than we do changes in our own social norms, and I find that just fascinating.”

Bender thinks the replicants could have done a better job of cleaning up all the external wires that are dangling in the L.A. of 2099. And Calo was amazed to see so many guns being used at the brink of the 22nd century. “It’s an incredibly old and savage technology … and the fact that they’re still using them is wild,” he says.

One thing I puzzled over: The replicants don’t seem to be networked together, and they’re not instantly able to identify or locate each other wirelessly. If I were a replicant overlord, that’s the first thing I’d do.

Looking beyond the techno-nitpicking, Bender says the “Blade Runner” franchise is notable in that it doesn’t have obvious good guys and bad guys. “We don’t want to actually map the replicants onto AIs in today’s parlance, so much as mapping the replicants onto other sentient beings in our midst that maybe we don’t understand so well, and that can include other people,” she says.

The first “Blade Runner” focused on whether machines could pass as humans, but the new “Blade Runner” flips the script. Could humans pass as machines? “That has really interesting resonances with what’s happening in our current situation with technology sold as AI, because so much of it is actually repurposing the work of people,” Bender says.

Bender doesn’t believe it’s possible for “Blade Runner 2099” to become reality, but Calo isn’t quite ready to rule that out entirely. “One thing about the esthetic of ‘Blade Runner’ is, it has this apocalyptic flavor to it … and this retrograde flavor to it. I think the only way we go from 2026 to 2099 and still have that is if something horribly calamitous happens in the interim,” Calo says.
“I hope we do get a world that is more civilized than what’s being depicted,” he says. “But we’ll see .”
Take a look at the original version of this item on Cosmic Log for reading recommendations from Emily M. Bender and Ryan Calo.

All eight episodes of “Blade Runner 2099” are showing on Amazon Prime. Stay tuned for future episodes of the Fiction Science podcast via Apple , Spotify , Player.fm , Pocket Casts and Podchaser . If you like Fiction Science, please rate the podcast and subscribe to get alerts for future episodes.

articles.title: Seattle skier vibe-codes ‘Pow Pow,’ a new snow report app that doesn’t sugarcoat the conditions
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Jeremy Sanford can’t control the weather that will hit ski resorts this winter, but he hopes his new app can at least tell you whether it’s worth loading up the car — or calling in sick.

Sanford, a senior product designer at Microsoft who grew up on the Eastside and has been skiing and snowboarding since he was a kid, has been building Pow Pow on nights and weekends, using “vibe coding” and Claude to do the work he couldn’t do himself.
The free app for iPhone and Android combines forecast data and readings from mountain snow sensors into snow reports for more than 200 resorts, from Snoqualmie Pass to Niseko, Japan.
Each resort gets a 1–5 “Pow Rating,” where a 5 means call in sick, and a blunt one-liner that says whether it really dumped overnight or your powder day is about to turn to rain.
For Sanford, the stakes come with a full car. He has two kids, ages 4 and 7, whom he is teaching to ski.
“I gotta load up the car with the kids and all the gear,” he said. “Is it just gonna be kind of crappy conditions when we get up there?”
He said none of the resort or weather apps he used gave him exactly what he wanted, and he didn’t fully trust the resorts’ numbers.
“You kind of got to take them with a grain of salt, because I feel like they inflate the numbers a little bit,” he said.

With Pow Pow, the aim is “an honest representation of what the conditions are actually like,” Sanford said. For the details, a section called “Nerd stuff” charts snowfall, base depth, snow quality, snow line, wind and UV.
“It’s got six inches of snow overnight, but what else is going on?” he said. “Oh, it’s maybe super wet up there now, and it’s supposed to be raining this afternoon.”

The headlines are where the app shows some attitude. The default version is family friendly, a second setting adds some profanity, and an “Unhinged” mode goes further. On a bluebird day with no new snow, the app might just tell you to “rip the groomers.”
Sanford said weather apps “can get redundant,” and he wanted “to just add a little bit of fun and add personality to it.”
A paid tier, Pow Pro, adds powder alerts, a 14-day outlook, resort webcams inside the app, home-screen widgets and the Unhinged headlines.
“Honestly, it’s a little bit of an experiment,” Sanford said. “If you could make a couple bucks off it on the side, great, but it’s not really the end goal.”
He got the idea in August, when he thought it would be cool to have “a ski app that I actually cared about” — one that looked and felt good.

Sanford has spent his career designing apps, not coding them. After graduating from Seattle Pacific University with a degree in visual communication design, he joined Microsoft in 2012, working on apps that shipped with Windows 8, including Weather, and later on the Microsoft Band. He spent nearly three years as a UX designer at Amazon, based in Edinburgh, Scotland, before returning to Microsoft in 2019. He now works on SharePoint.
“I don’t have a background in coding or engineering, and so there was always kind of like a hump … a barrier to entry,” he said. AI tools were “the unlock for me to actually make something real.”
Claude did much of the heavy lifting. “Claude and I are buddies,” Sanford said.

Next up, he’s experimenting with a feature that would recommend gear based on the day’s conditions, such as a powder board, a darker lens for better visibility, or extra layers if it’s going to get colder in the afternoon. He’s also asking skiers and snowboarders to send feedback through the app.

A good read on conditions could matter more than usual this winter. A very strong El Niño, possibly a record-setter, is building in the Pacific, and NOAA’s outlook favors a warmer-than-normal winter for the Pacific Northwest.

Meteorologist Larry Schick, who writes the Powder Poobah forecast, wrote last month that the season won’t be a bust. But he expects a slow start, with warm early storms and high snow levels, and warned that skiers “may have to pivot quickly and cherry pick” the best days.
Sanford is “cautiously optimistic” about the season. He has seven or eight resorts pinned to his phone’s home screen, webcams included.
“Hopefully this year is decent,” he said. “The last year was not amazing.”

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Aventide builds AI client management software for consultants and coaches
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Christian Quiver and Eric Baxter met in a grocery store parking lot, introduced by their wives. Quiver needed a designer for a project, so the two swapped numbers and agreed to try working together for 90 days. Four years later, they’re building a startup together in the Columbia River Gorge.

Their startup, Aventide , opened to the public on Oct. 29. It’s AI-powered software for consultants, coaches and others who sell their expertise one client at a time. Aventide drafts proposals, invoices and follow-ups, but nothing goes to a client until the owner approves it.
The name blends “abhainn,” the Irish Gaelic word for river, with “tide,” for the spot where a river meets the sea and where towns and ports have long grown up.

Quiver, the CEO, lives in White Salmon, Wash., and spent more than five years at Amazon. He led go-to-market for the in-store experience as Amazon’s device stores grew from two locations to 50. Baxter is chief design officer and lives in nearby Trout Lake. He spent 25 years in product design, including nearly seven years leading user experience at Welocalize, whose clients included Amazon, Google and Apple.

The idea started in 2025 with a question from Baxter’s wife: Which part of his decades of designing products for other people actually brought him joy? His answer was helping people, especially those pushed out by AI-era layoffs who were trying to start something of their own. Quiver bought in that October.

The pair spent more than six months testing with three groups of business owners in the Gorge, including at a demo day in June with the Mid-Columbia Innovation Hub. They kept meeting people who live in small towns and sell their expertise to companies in Seattle or Portland. “A consultant in a small town can land a corporate client,” Quiver said in an email.

The two-person company is bootstrapped and says 81 people are using Aventide so far. After a 14-day free trial, plans cost $39 or $99 a month. Aventide also publishes estimates of the electricity and water behind everyday tasks in the app. Quiver says the figures could be off by a factor of two either way. “If you ask what it costs in electricity and water to use our product, you get a straight answer,” he said.
We caught up with Quiver for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch?

Aventide is an AI-native client management platform for people paid by the session, project or event. It replaces separate booking, proposal, contract, portal and invoice apps, and runs more than one business from one login.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?
Tool fragmentation in small client businesses, and the fact that the owner ends up being the human glue holding all of it together.
What surprised you after talking to customers?
That the barrier isn’t price or features. People don’t have time to switch systems, and many aren’t comfortable with their own software stack. So we onboard anyone who wants it one-on-one.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

Everything. It has fundamentally changed what a small team can build and run. We have always worked as experience builders first, and AI lets a team of two think bigger, test faster, and deliver a world-class product that would have taken what seems like 100-200 people just a year or two ago. It cuts our time from idea to execution by at least 50x.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

People hear “AI for small business” and picture a chat box taped onto legacy software. Instead of making you click through old CRM menus with a writing bot on the side, Aventide wires AI directly into your bookings, contracts, portals, and payments so you just say it, review it and approve.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Choosing which problem we wanted to solve. Our original mission was far too vague to build. We set out to help people through the AI era, but the interviews and prototypes kept landing on client services. Following that meant narrowing a big mission into one product for one kind of owner.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Think bigger, and focus on the whole experience you want to create. Outside of a few rare cases, narrow single-purpose tools are old hat now because nobody wants another tab to manage. The future belongs to software where someone can say, “This is my one tool for this category of my life.
50,000 human-scale businesses use Aventide to own their client relationships directly, keeping more money in small businesses and giving more time back to the people running them.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Holiday Buses and Trains
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The holiday season is upon us and there are few better ways to celebrate than on board a historic transit vehicle. This year, the Metro Employees Historic Vehicle Association’s (MEHVA) Holiday Lights Tour is on December 5. Climb aboard a preserved Metro bus and enjoy a trip through several Seattle neighborhoods to see the best holiday lights in the City. The 2 hour tour starts at 7pm, one block east of Stadium station. Tickets and more information can be found on MEHVA’s website .

Between now and December 23, Mt. Rainier Scenic Railroad is running the Steam Into Christmas experience. The 75-minute journey/show takes place on vintage passenger cars pulled by either the 104-year-old Polson Logging No. 70 or the 102-year-old Porter No. 5 locomotive. Trips run every Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, as well as on December 21-23. Trains depart from the Elbe Depot, located about a 2-hour drive south of Seattle. Unfortunately, the depot is not accessible via transit. Tickets and more information can be found on Mt. Rainier Scenic Railroad’s website .

articles.title: Harborview Injury Center Recommends Nightly E-Scooter Curfew
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A prominent Seattle injury research center is advocating for changes to how e-scooter rentals are regulated, presenting recommendations last week that included a full nighttime curfew on the devices, along with better age verification. The recommendations come in response to increased rates of injuries from scooter users over recent years, particularly within cities where usage has spiked as Lime-operated bikes, scooters, and gliders have grown ubiquitous.

The data presented by Dr. Frederick P. Rivara of Harborview's Injury Research & Prevention Center shows a dramatic increase in e-scooter related emergency responses since the launch of Seattle's first free-floating scooter share program in 2020. In 2025, 517 emergency responses related to e-scooters were recorded citywide, the highest one-year total on file. That increase has occurred against a dramatic scale-up in overall usage, with Lime recording more than 10 million trips citywide across the same 12 months.
The King County Board of Health, which reviewed Rivara's data on November 19, has not yet acted on the recommendations, and hasn't put the issue of e-scooter safety on its future work plan.

When they do occur, e-scooter injuries can be devastating. A separate, newly-released study led by UW Medicine looking at 64 e-scooter riders treated at Harborview between 2020 and 2024 found that the median amount of lost time at work due to recovery time was two months, with 20% forced to change jobs as a result of their crash.

"This is a problem that all big cities that have these devices are really struggling with," Rivara said, citing a nearly decade-old study from Austin, Texas that found that e-scooter injury rates were roughly 175 to 200 times higher on a per-mile basis than trips in motor vehicles.

The dramatic recommendation for a 9pm to 5am curfew, made in coordination with Rivara's research partners Xinyao de Grauw and Stephen J. Mooney, comes from analysis of statewide surveillance data on bike and scooter usage. Compared to e-bike injuries, which tend to occur during commuting hours or at mid-day, e-scooter injuries are highly prevalent on weekend nights, according to the data.

"The hours of the day are important, and that's why we are proposing a curfew at those times a day," Rivara said. "Overall, I think that 38% of the injuries from e-scooters are happening after 9 p.m."

Rivera pointed to two studies showing positive impacts from nighttime scooter curfews, one from Atlanta and one from Helsinki. In Helsinki, the curfew was only in effect on Friday and Saturday night from 12am to 5am, with significant restrictions on top speeds added during the overnight hours on other days. The result was a 39% decrease in injuries from one year to the next.

Atlanta's 9pm scooter curfew, implemented in 2019, showed much less clear results, and has been gradually scaled back to a current 2am to 4am curfew. A 2021 study on the changes did find a decrease in injuries, but its researchers labelled the decrease "not significant." What was seen in Atlanta, however, was a spike in vehicle usage , indicating that many e-scooter users had been using the devices to replace car trips. Average commute times shot up by around 10%, with travel times to stadium events such as soccer games increasing by almost 12 minutes per trip.

A discussion around trade-offs that could come with such a curfew was absent from Rivara's presentation, with potential issues around mobility impacts brushed aside as he asserted that such a curfew would have a "minimal impact on use of these devices for commuting."

E-scooters are widely used across Seattle to bridge gaps in transit service, particularly later in the evening when such a curfew would be in effect. With only a limited number of buses running a full 24 hours and Sound Transit light rail service shutting off before 1 am, Lime often offers the easiest option for travel during those hours, including for workers in service industry jobs or with non-traditional working hours.
A curfew, especially one starting as early as 9pm, would be a dramatic change, and one that several members of the King County Board of Health pushed back on.

"Nine o'clock seems very early to eliminate the accessibility of these devices for people who are commuting. So I'd like your body of of experts to consider moving that curfew to a later time," said Katherine Gudgel, Director of Community Programs at HealthPoint, in comments that were echoed by Seattle Councilmember Dionne Foster.
"I think there's a lot of folks that work late that may use this, [I'm] especially thinking about folks in the hospitality industry," Burien Councilmember Hugo Garcia said.
Unsurprisingly, Lime isn't on board with the idea either.

"We don’t think a blanket 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew is the right approach for Seattle. That’s an eight-hour restriction that would affect evening and early-morning commutes, including people working shifts that don’t fit a nine-to-five schedule," Parker Dawson, Lime's Senior Regional Lead of Government Relations for the Pacific Northwest, told The Urbanist. "Before taking away a transportation option for those hours, we need to understand who relies on it and what alternatives they actually have."
In a letter sent this week in response to the Board of Health presentation, Dawson noted that its incident rate per one million Lime rides in Seattle declined 26.6% between 2024 and 2025.

"We’ve heard from Seattle riders that Lime helps many of them with their commutes and everyday travel," Dawson continued. "Riders told us about getting home safely after missing the last bus and feeling safer riding home than walking alone at night. One described taking Lime home from the light rail station rather than waiting 30 minutes for a bus. Those experiences help explain how Lime complements transit: it makes the trip to or from a station easier and fills gaps when bus service is limited or has stopped for the night."

Rivara's recommendations also included more robust age-verification requirements for e-scooter rentals, given that Harborview's data shows that youth account for 15% of micromobility admissions seen at trauma centers. On that front, Lime points to age-verification requirements already in place when it comes to payment methods used on its app, which are supplemented by education campaigns. But overhauls in this area are likely to be much less controversial, with a bill introduced at the New York City Council just this month that would require more direct age verification for riders of CitiBike, the primary bikeshare provider in the Big Apple.

When it comes to an overnight curfew, however, a more convincing case may need to be made for such a significant overhaul of Seattle's existing e-scooter regulations, with Lime providing thousands of late night and early morning rides every single day. Turning that off would be much more complicated than simply hitting a switch, and likely lead to countless unintended consequences.

articles.title: Manion Task Force Calls for Changes to Involuntary Treatment
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: When she first ran for office back in 2022, King County Prosecuting Attorney Leesa Manion made a promise to work to reimagine the system around Washington State’s Involuntary Treatment Act (ITA). Earlier this month, soon after winning another four-year term, Manion’s task force released a report of findings and recommendations for improving the system.

The report, written by the Chuckanut Health Foundation, based its findings on a wide-ranging listening tour that conducted 47 conversations about the ITA in Whatcom County, King County, Spokane, and the Greater Columbia region. The listening tour included feedback from people who had been involuntarily committed, their families and friends, mental health professionals and crisis responders, law enforcement, and both prosecutors and defense attorneys.

The cross-disciplinary task force conducted the listening tour. In addition to representation from two prosecutor’s offices, it included members from the Washington Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs (WASPC), Disability Rights Washington, the Snohomish County Office of Public Defense, and the Health and Justice Recovery Alliance.
Manion talked with The Urbanist about what led her to start the project.

“It wasn't lost on me that a lot of what we were seeing in our community that people were describing as public safety issues were really a very specific type of mental health issue,” Manion said. “One of the things that's always kind of frustrated me about the current involuntary treatment at court system, and I can really only speak firsthand to King County, is just how litigious it is and how adversarial it is. I thought, rather than have a prosecutor fighting for someone's treatment against their will and a public defender fighting for that person's release to the streets, two very binary choices, what would it look like if we could reimagine the system writ large so that it was more collaborative?”

Involuntary treatment is mandated by state law if a person is considered to be a threat to themselves or others. This kind of forced treatment is generally a last resort for a person experiencing an acute mental crisis, and it’s the best resourced component of the state’s mental health system. In fact, the report found that in King County, people were describing involuntary treatment as a kind of a back door to treatment that people couldn’t otherwise afford.

It’s also the most restrictive and costly way to treat patients with behavioral health issues. Being pushed into involuntary treatment tends to be very disruptive to a patient’s daily life, interrupting employment, education, care-giving, housing, and access to benefits, and it’s not uncommon for a patient to cycle through the system, sometimes multiple times.
Kim Mosolf, an attorney with the advocacy organization Disability Rights Washington who participated in the work group, explained some of the problems coercion can cause around getting care.

“It oftentimes will make people less likely to engage in care in the long term,” Mosolf said. “It increases senses of stigma and self-stigma, which then lead to poorer outcomes on discharge. There's a lot of data, and it also has obvious destabilizing effects: You lose your job, you lose your home, you lose your custody. These are all things you could face. You lose other civil rights because of an involuntary civil commitment.”
Mosolf said that putting someone into involuntary civil commitment is no guarantee that they will get better.

“We hear from folks who with lived experience who've had really negative experiences with either trying to access care or being pushed into forced treatment, or you know, having really, really bad experiences like abuse within forced treatment and never really feeling like they're being listened to or cared for in any real way,” Mosolf said.
The report presents three broad recommendations that received support from across participating stakeholders:

Resourcing the continuum of care would mean a greater focus both on prevention before a person reaches a crisis point and on continued support being in place after being released from commitment. Right now patients are often released into “nothing,” the report said.

“Washington’s ITA system is built to step in at the moment of crisis, and then to send people back into a community that often lacks both what would have prevented the crisis and what would sustain recovery after it,” the report continued. “The ITA is asked, in effect, to be the front door, the emergency room, and the discharge plan for a behavioral health system that is thin at both ends. Almost every vantage point describes this, each in its own words, as a loop that keeps producing the same outcomes no matter how hard the people inside it work.”

Aleksandra Letts, a senior deputy prosecuting attorney with King County, explained that the goal of having the ITA applied to fewer people could potentially be achieved “if we have better wraparound services to prevent people from entering the ITA system because they can get community support and to have them have all of the services when they're exiting and they're being discharged into something that's not nothing, which unfortunately happens too often now.”

Meanwhile, the scarcity of beds and resources in the continuum of care makes it difficult to ensure appropriate treatment options are available to patients. There is a particular lack of beds in rural areas of the state, as well as a lack of beds for patients with specific needs, such as youth and individuals with other major medical issues.

“Often, when bed dates are unavailable, first responders are forced to rely on other systems to provide immediate support such as emergency rooms, jails, shelters, or unprepared family members,” the report read.

Addressing both of these recommendations would require further investment at a time when both the state and local municipalities are grappling with budget deficits. While some investments could potentially be shifted over time from involuntary treatment to both preventative care and support provided after release, such a redistribution would likely require bridge funding while the system shifts.

“We are already spending money on the system,” Manion said. “We already have folks who are leaving the ITA system and sometimes moving over to the carceral system, or they are moving over to a hospital system, and all of that is expensive. But we're not really tracking the dollars in any kind of meaningful connect-the-dot ways, and we're not getting the return on investment that we would hope.”
Mosolf emphasized that in the long term, a system focused on the entire continuum of care is likely to be cheaper.

“If you actually invest in these things that we're recommending, you're hopefully going to save money,” Mosolf said. “Things like permanent supportive housing cost money upfront, but they are shown to vastly reduce people's engagement with being arrested, going to the ER, being placed in civil commitment, which costs a ton of money, so it pays off. It saves money, but you have to be willing to recognize that and shift those funds and wait for the payoff.”
One of the biggest barriers to changing the ITA system as it currently stands is the lack of data about how it’s working.

“We know nothing about ITA. Nothing,” Jason Schwartz, the director of the Snohomish County Office of Public Defense, told The Urbanist . “We don't even know how many cases were filed across the state. We don't know how many had public defenders, how many had private lawyers. We don't know why they were detained, and I think that's really important because someone who is just gravely disabled, unable to take care of themselves, is very different than someone who's a danger to others.”
State authorities do not have a reliable count of how many people are cycling repeatedly through the system nor data showing the most common uses of the system.
“The fact that there's not a statewide system where someone can plug in someone's name and determine what their mental health intervention trajectory has been is really shocking,” Letts said.

Manion explained that right now, there isn’t even consensus on which data should be gathered. Figuring out what statewide data standards should be implemented and figuring out how to improve communication between silos engaged in the system is work that could be done right away without a high price tag.

Another place where there was agreement across the work group was that now is not the time to change the legal threshold where the ITA kicks in. While opinions differ on whether it should be easier or more difficult to commit someone, workgroup members agreed that there are several compelling reasons to wait. The lack of available data on how the ITA system is working makes it difficult to know what changes might be appropriate, and the current system is already stretched and overburdened. In addition, if the report’s recommendations were to be implemented, that might shift the system to the point that no legal change is required.
“If we change the standard now, it's going to create a burden on a system that we already don't fully understand,” Schwartz said.

“I think part of it is just making sure before we make a big change like the standard, the entry standard, that we do a good job, a diligent job, of funding the resources that would make it so that people don't have to go to ITA, so they can be successful when they leave, and so that we know what we're doing before we make any real substantive changes,” Manion said.
The task force report made several near-term recommendations for 2027 and 2028 with a focus on the state legislature.

In addition to asking that the legislature not make any cuts to already existing programs and investments in the continuum of care, the report called for progress to be made on improved data reporting on ITA system performance so policy makers can gain a better sense of how the system is currently functioning.

Another recommendation was to begin a two-year study on how insurance status affects how patients receive voluntary versus involuntary care and review and make recommendations on Medicaid and crisis response reimbursement rate increases.

The report also called for the funding of one pilot program in 2027 and two pilots in 2028 that would work to promote safe information sharing in patient care with families and peer supports and implement more intensive discharge planning to provide more ongoing support once a patient is discharged.

“The pilot is really designed to kick the tires on an idea to see what's working and to test a theory,” Manion said. “So, if our theory is: by treating people coming out of the system in a way that is more robust, more consistent, more patient-centered, will we get better results, I think we expect the answer to be yes, but we're not doing that right now.”
The hope is that the state legislature will be able to fund such a pilot, but Manion said if not, she’ll look into whether it’s plausible to use King County funds from the Crisis Care Centers Levy .

“I think if we implement the data and upstream and downstream resources, I do think that what this will help us do is dispel some myths about ITA and really build some empathy around the people who need empathy in the ITA system,” Schwartz said.
Task force members emphasized that making progress on these short-term recommendations would put the state on track to implementing some of the bigger aspirational goals highlighted in the report.
“There's a lot of uncontroversial agreement on what we can do better to start to fix some of these problems,” Mosolf said. “I think we know the solutions so that should give everybody some solace.”

articles.title: Why is Seattle’s socialist, renter mayor so focused on a balanced budget?
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It is not a typical Thanksgiving message from a Seattle leader. Mayor Katie Wilson is defending her push for a balanced budget while looking back on a fall City Hall battle she did not fully win.
Why is Seattle’s socialist, renter mayor so focused on fiscal restraint?

“Fiscal responsibility is a progressive value,” Wilson said in a video address ahead of the holiday. “For too long that phrase has been code for slashing public services. That is emphatically not what Seattle stands for.”

Following the Seattle City Council’s approval of the 2027–2028 budget , Wilson this week is defending her plan to close a projected $175 million deficit through spending efficiencies rather than tax hikes, arguing that prudent management sustains public services. Acknowledging that her four-year balanced proposal surprised both progressive critics and business leaders, she insisted that public trust depends on responsible stewardship.
So why is Wilson echoing a George H.W. Bush -level “no new taxes” stance?

First, there is the JumpStart payroll tax to protect. Wilson opted against raising JumpStart on large corporations amid downtown office vacancies and tech-sector uncertainty, instead pairing internal efficiencies with an August revenue bump to fund core social investments. At the same time, she pushed back against the council’s move to raid $31 million in JumpStart reserves — originally intended for affordable housing and post-pandemic services — to pay for council amendments.

Second, her fiscal discipline flipped traditional political roles at City Hall. During negotiations, the centrist-leaning council, led by Budget Chair Dan Strauss , added roughly $36 million in General Fund spending, including $31 million in one-time funds, to reverse several of Wilson’s cuts. Although the council prevailed, Wilson cast herself as the disciplined executive pushing back against unsustainable budget stuffing.

“One-time funds set expectations for additional funding in future years—funding that does not exist,” she warned, adding that she will instead pursue new progressive revenue, including a local capital gains tax, in Olympia.

Over the longer term, Wilson’s posture also shapes debates over policing and future deficits. By backing funding to bring the Seattle Police Department to 1,250 officers, she aims to meet realistic hiring targets while blunting “defund” attacks and tempering demands for higher staffing thresholds from council public safety chair — and potential future mayoral challengers — Bob Kettle . Meanwhile, the council’s reliance on one-time reserve sweeps to restore encampment and clearance programs creates a looming fiscal cliff unless Olympia approves new taxing authority or local revenues rebound.

In 2027, Wilson’s political capital will be tested in Olympia, where lawmakers remain wary of expanding municipal tax powers amid state budget pressures. At home, police hiring numbers and the rollout of CARE crisis response teams will test whether her holistic safety approach can satisfy downtown businesses without alienating her progressive base.

Those fights will unfold ahead of a major structural shift. Seattle’s inaugural ranked-choice voting primary will take place next August for all seven district council seats. By allowing voters to rank up to five candidates, ranked-choice voting could reduce the spoiler dynamic that has previously split progressive coalitions. The result could be a council that leans even farther left — and aligns more fully with Wilson’s administration.
One big change for the council can already by marked. Wilson is celebrating incoming District 5 Councilmember Nilu Jenks as part of a new “progressive majority” across the city — and the nation.

Armed with early wins like universal school meals and the positioning in fiscal discipline, Wilson is set to back aligned challengers and further reshape the council. For now, she is keeping balanced budgets at the center of her message.
“Overall we have made meaningful progress this year toward a structurally balanced budget,” Wilson said, “and I look forward to completing that work in the years ahead.”

articles.title: Mossback's Northwest: Abby Hill. Have Paintbox, Will Travel.
articles.author: Knute Berger
paras: This scratched paint box was a ticket to freedom for one woman. It was filled—and is still filled—with some of the tools of the artist who carried it with her into the Western wilderness to capture its beauty and wildness on canvas for posterity: her tubes of paint, a brush, a palette for mixing colors. It traveled with her deep into the mountains, it sat with her easel on precipitous cliffs, it banged along on horseback on remote trails.

Abby Williams Hill moved to the Northwest—to Tacoma—in 1889. She was a white, Iowa-raised middle class woman who was a trained artist. Her husband Frank Hill was a respectable doctor who set up a practice there. But Abby eschewed city life in the budding “City of Destiny.” She refused to wear corsets and bustles. She wanted to dress in practical garb, like a man. She refused to let domestic life or her husband or her stuffy Victorian peers hold her back from places where her spirit soared.
From her first hike to Mount Rainier she knew her art and inspiration—and she herself—belonged in wild country. And that she could capture it for the rest of us on canvas.
This battered tin box helped make that possible.

Abby Williams Hill was a woman of her time, though she often felt out of step with the mainstream. She wanted change and reform. She was devoted to social progress and to conservation. She met President Teddy Roosevelt at the White House in 1902 while visiting with a delegation from the Congress of Mothers and he gave her a white rose which she later painted. She advocated creating a safety net for the poor. She devoted time to childhood education—she was a founder the PTA in Washington. She homeschooled her own children, four of them--a disabled son and three adopted daughters.

She wanted the freedom from being a prisoner of fashion. When her husband encouraged her to wear a corset, she dared him to wear one for a day and then ask her. He did, and afterwards he dropped the subject. Some believe she was not enthusiastic about women’s suffrage, though she was strong-minded, an independent spirit.

A turning point in her life, after years of caring for her son who was born with a disability, was to experience the grand nature of the West. In July of 1895, she signed up for a group hike on Mt. Rainier, or Mt. Tacoma as she called it. Her co-ed group spent six days just getting there by wagon, then some continued on horseback up to Camp of the Clouds at Paradise. It was cold, the ground was rough, the sound of calving glaciers and rushing water were the trip’s soundtrack.

She did not want her time at Camp of the Clouds to end. “The night was bitter cold,” she wrote in her journal. “All were quite ready to go home in the morning but me. I felt I could endure much more for a few days of such grandeur.”

Within two weeks of returning home, she set out on a 12-day camping expedition to Hood Canal. Later, she had a routine of rowing to Vashon Island where she set up camp with her kids and spent summers. “I was cut out for the wilds,” she reflected.

Abby the painter wanted to be in nature but also wanted to share it with those who couldn’t be there in person. She had a growing reputation—she had done an image of George Washington exhibited at the World’s Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago and later exhibited her works at other major expositions including ones at Jamestown, St. Louis, Portland, and Seattle.

From 1903 to 1906, she made the first of an incredible series of arrangements—especially for a woman artist—with the Great Northern and Northern Pacific Railroads. In exchange for 1,000 miles of free tickets, leaving her husband behind, she and her children would travel to parks and wild areas the railroads wanted to promote and paint landscapes that could be used to bring views of the rugged West to the public and promote tourism. Have paintbox, will travel.

Abby was what is called an "en plein air" painter who worked not in a studio but outdoors where nature’s light, shifting weather and textures were part of the landscape she tried to capture. Her training was both traditional and contemporary. One of her teacher’s was William Merritt Chase who she studied with in New York. He was a leading American proponent of Impressionism which influenced her work. He was impressed with her talent and “her genius for work.” She and her husband also traveled extensively in Europe on a tandem bike.

Her work came at a time when photography was in ascendence. But her landscapes could capture color, magic moments, rare and spectacular views. She chased morning and evening light to catch transcendent moments. Her train commissions took her from Mt. Rainier to the North Cascades and Chelan, to Yellowstone, Flathead Lake and the Clark Fork in Montana, and gorges in Idaho. She could paint when and how she chose, including roughing it in the back country where the Hills might be plagued by rain, wind, biting bugs and rattlesnakes.

An example of the dangers: while painting on a cliff’s edge at Yellowstone Falls, a sudden squall caused her and her daughter Eulalie to scramble to get their gear and themselves to safety. Te whirlwind took the canvas she was painting and sailed it over the cliff’s edge—a precious work lost. The next day, a local guide tied a rope to a tree and around his waist and climbed 100 feet down a 400-foot chasm and recovered the picture. It was worse for wear: wet, covered with sand and dust. Abby reckoned it was worth a $1,000 and a difficult image to capture. To the railroad it might be worth $10,000 in advertising.
It has been noted that her work was a kind of contradiction. The nature she sought to capture was being transformed by the railroads that paid her fares. Still, they enabled her access and art.

After her days of railroading, she traveled the country, painting largely in the southwest at places like Zion, Bryce, the Grand Canyon, Yosemite, the beaches and redwoods of California. She and Frank took a multi-year road trip across America in 1924, and settled in southern California, but maintained a residence in Tacoma.

Her work is a marvelous window on the West and her vigorous life. An exceptional thing she did left a mark on the map. While working for the Great Northern in 1903 she ventured into the North Cascades along the Stehekin River above Lake Chelan where she came across an impressive peak that she discovered had no official name. Abby decided to name it—which she did successfully. It’s Mt. Booker, named for Booker T. Washington, a Black educator who Abby knew and admired. She painted the peak for posterity, a tribute to the wild land and the better world she worked for.

articles.title: ‘Genuinely emotional’: the world-conquering Chicken Shop Date’s final, eye-opening episode
articles.author: Stuart Heritage
paras: After a 12-year run, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s last episode of Chicken Shop Date – a therapy session with Esther Perel – is being shown in cinemas. It’s a fittingly grand finale for a YouTube cult favourite that far outgrew its medium

The decision to screen the full final series of Chicken Shop Date in cinemas before the finale airs on YouTube is, it could be argued, overkill. The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say.

And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. After 12 years of flirting and awkwardness, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s final guest is Esther Perel, the Belgian psychotherapist and relationship guru beloved by Oprah Winfrey. It is by no means a traditional episode, almost completely dismissing the tone of everything that came before it. Dimoldenberg’s well-honed persona, alternately dismissive and needy, is nowhere to be seen. Instead, Dimoldenberg does something that Perel must be deadeningly familiar with when meeting new people: she uses the episode as a free therapy session.

paras: German model and artist whose bold and dynamic shoots made her one of the biggest stars of 1960s fashion
The aspiring model Vera von Lehndorff created “Veruschka” – little Vera – as a memorable alternative persona whose existence was performance art.

She used her natural resources: a 6ft-plus-tall body that, horizontal, could fill an entire glossy magazine spread; a face with magnificent bone architecture and feline eyes; and a long mane that was amenable to brutal short cuts and extraordinary coiffures. All were animated by her instinct for making shapes in air – not a model’s poses but a dancer’s movements that only a click of the lens could catch. Watch her seducing the camera of the photographer, played by David Hemmings , in Michelangelo Antonioni ’s 1966 film Blow Up to see her original act in action.

articles.title: ‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: Some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “ Metroidvania ” or “ Soulslike .” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

Aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel , with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

It’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of New York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

No matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

If you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.
Aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

articles.title: Elevated line to Ballard
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting somebody asked whether Sound Transit had considered elevating the line instead of tunneling to reduce cost and build it earlier. Sound Transit’s response was that they cannot imagine any way to build an elevated Link light rail line through downtown and meet current environmental requirements. An elevated line would certainly be cheaper and faster to build and easier for riders to access than the currently planned deep tunnel. Could any of the alternative modes I described make it possible to build an elevated line through downtown?

As Kubly/Reed recently pointed out, current Link trains needs very long stations. That makes it difficult to find a location for an underground station which does not interfere with existing building foundations, but also to fit an elevated station into the existing street valleys. For more infrequent lines, the station also has to allow sufficient waiting area requiring wider platforms. As Kubly/Reed pointed out, automated light metro systems allow more frequent but shorter trains which reduces the size of the station area. Link also requires a pole for overhead wires, an emergency and maintenance walkway, and potentially noise barriers along its guideway for a total width of about 29 feet . Link’s maximum turn radius (82 feet) and maximum grade (6%) also create challenges to fit the guideway into downtown. Monorail guideways are visually less bulky but still require a separate emergency walkway. When the Monorail Project suggested running the Green Line through downtown as an elevated line, people were also concerned about their privacy as riders may peek into their windows. Link would require an even wider guideway than the monorail.

Modern guideways such as used by TSB Maglev integrate the emergency walkway into the middle of the track rather than between the two tracks and only require a 20 feet wide guideway. With a center platform, a station requires a width of 50 feet (60′ for Link). To scale Seattle’s hills, grades of up to 10% can be handled. Construction is much faster and less disruptive as the guideway is prefabricated. Once the columns are built, the guideway gets trucked in and placed by crane.
Various elevated alignments have been considered in the past (or should be):

Modern maglev guideway technology may also make it feasible to run along 15th Ave W through Interbay and use precast modules for a station above the road. As such technology also allows for grades up to 10%, it may even allow a bridge over the ship canal. Otherwise a ship canal tunnel would still be required unless Sound Transit would consider a Salmon Bay gondola for now and save even more.

The downtown alignments could also be used to connect with the West Seattle line. The First Hill alignments would create a great alternative if the current downtown tunnel is out of service, with transfers at Westlake and Mt. Baker.
Elevated guideways also make it much easier to add branches (for example to serve Aurora Ave) or add a station later – practically impossible in case of a drilled tunnel.

While an elevated line would be far cheaper, it would probably require a new EIS submission. That would add a few years to the timeline, but because of the lower cost, construction could start immediately once federal approval has been obtained. That may still allow an opening date closer to the 2032 target date than waiting until 2060 and we would not have to burden our grandchildren with paying off a much larger debt.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Emerald City Trail Is an Ideal Guide to Seattle’s Olmsted History
articles.author: Valentina Vaneeva
paras: While our region is famous for its beautiful outdoors, driving for an hour or more or carrying a backpack should not be a prerequisite for taking a nice long walk and enjoying the views. But figuring out where to go in the city is sometimes frustrating if you want to avoid getting stuck in a rut, with every intersection presenting yet another choice. And so it is always a joy when a new guidebook falls into your hands.

Emerald City Trail: A Walking Guide Through Seattle & Our Olmsted History , written by Peter Hendrickson of Seattle Mountaineers and published this year by Mountaineers Books, is unique in its goal of not just making your life easier by giving you directions but also tying the routes to one particular piece of Seattle history: its connection to Olmsted Brothers , heirs of the Olmsted of New York’s Central Park fame.

It is not a history book, but it gives enough of an overview of how the brothers played a role in shaping the city, and there is enough to keep your walks interesting. For those who want to learn more, the Resources section at the end of the book will be helpful.

Emerald City Trail is a 75-mile loop connecting both existing and proposed parks and boulevards that were elements of the plan developed by Olmsted Brothers for the City of Seattle at the start of the 20th century. The whole loop is conveniently split into 12 segments, 5 to 7.5 miles long, with options to shorten or lengthen any one of them, and their start and end points are accessible by transit. The guidebook also recommends detours for those with a stroller if the original route has stairs or difficult terrain.

Each section's description has a route map with viewpoints and landmarks and lists the usual stats of distance, elevation, and difficulty, but what sets this guidebook apart is that it also mentions the “Three Ts”: public transportation, public toilets and treats, that is, cafes, bakeries, bars or ice cream shops. Having such conveniences at hand lightens the load you need to carry and leaves you free to stray off route at will.

The book is of a small size and can be used for navigation directly, but you may prefer following its companion interactive map at emeraldcitytrail.com since it shows your actual location and has a built-in transit layer. Depending on your screen size, you may not find the interface very convenient and may prefer to download the GPX file of the whole loop or a segment you're interested in to be used with a navigation app of your choice.

Despite what the book says, at the time of this writing, you cannot download GPX tracks from its companion website, but they are available from the Mountaineers website ; scroll past the description and click on the “Resources” section.

This Mountaineers page also lists upcoming walks for sections of the route, so if you are looking for company or want to meet the author, you can sign up for one. Additionally, you can look up recent trip reports, and this too sets the book apart from other urban walking guidebooks because each segment has a Mountaineer steward who walks their section at least quarterly to spot safety or maintenance issues.

The guidebook also highlights difficulties walking in some parts of Seattle for which geography cannot be blamed . The route of Section 6, Rainier Beach to White Center, is the most challenging part of Emerald City Trail. Since it goes through an industrial area, there is not much shade, few restrooms and food options, but plenty of high-speed traffic and tricky highway crossings. Indeed, the author recommends avoiding the most unsafe crossing altogether and catching a bus instead, which is something you cannot do on a regular hike even if you bring your Orca transit card.
Compare that to Section 2, Woodland Park Zoo to Husky Stadium, which goes through a park and along tree-lined streets and has plenty of opportunity for treats on the way.

I am yet to complete the whole 75 miles of the loop, in fact, I have just started, but I like that the route gives you an enjoyable mix of nature, art, historic landmarks and people watching. And, as Hendrickson promised, on our very first walk, when we stopped for a coffee break, we met someone interesting to talk with.

If this sounds like something you might like, this guidebook is for you. And if not, perhaps fantastic photos by Heidi Walker will inspire you to explore one of the sections. And don't let the Big Dark scare you into staying home. Worst case, you can always take a bus or a train and bail out, just don't forget your Orca card!

articles.title: Sound Transit Debuts Refurbished Kinkisharyo Link Trains
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: This morning, Sound Transit quietly launched the first refurbished Kinkisharyo trainset on the 2 Line. After years of design and months of testing, light-rail vehicles 110 and 113 ran a roundtrip between Redmond and Lynnwood during the morning rush hour. Part of the initial Link fleet delivered in 2006, these vehicles have been out of service for a deep refurbishment that saw upgrades to the train’s electrical and communication systems.

In 2022, Sound Transit contracted Woojin IS America to refresh the 62 Kinkisharyo trains, also knows as Series 1. These trains were delivered between 2006 and 2011 and include some now-outdated components. Replacing these will allow the vehicles to remain in a state of good repair for the next 15 years. Many of the upgrades are out-of-sight from passengers, including new operator controls, automated passenger counters (APC) in every car, upgraded CCTV cameras, and an ethernet-based networking system.

Passengers will notice a few changes on the refurbished KI trains. The exterior-facing displays now show the line color and number. Inside the train, the dot matrix displays have been replaced by the screens that show the next few stops. These screens are slightly different from those on Series 2 trains, and do not show connections to other transit routes. Three lights have been added around each door. The lights flash blue when the door will open soon and change color to green when the door is open. The onboard speakers have been upgraded to provide clearer announcements. These trains also allow the Link Control Center to make remote announcements when needed. A video of the PA system and door lights in action is available here .

Four of the 62 Series 1 LRVs have completed the retrofit and two more are currently undergoing the retrofit process. The remaining 56 LRVs will be upgraded over the next three years. Retrofitted LRVs are not compatible with original Series 1 LRVs, so the number of upgraded trainsets in use will be limited until more cars complete the retrofitting process. For the foreseeable future, expect to see the new trains Monday-Friday on block 53 in the morning and block 54 in the afternoon. For the exact timings of each block, refer to the schedule on Pantograph .
