articles.title: Why expect holiday traditions to stay the same, even as life continually changes?
articles.author:
<name>Lee Ann Rawlins Williams, Clinical Assistant Professor of Education, Health and Behavior Studies, University of North Dakota</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/lee-ann-rawlins-williams-1486589"/>
paras: There’s something about the holiday season that makes people notice the passage of time. As you unpack treasured decorations, prepare family recipes and listen to familiar holiday songs, you’re reminded not only of celebrations from years past but also of different times in your life.

With each passing year, children grow older, families welcome new members, relationships change, and some of those you once celebrated with are no longer here. But people often approach the holidays hoping to experience them just as they once did.

As someone who studies life transitions , I’m particularly interested in why people expect traditional holiday celebrations to remain the same when so much else in life has changed. I suggest thinking of holiday memories not as a blueprint for recreating the past but as a way to understand what makes these times meaningful to you, and how you might carry that meaning into the present.

Research on family rituals suggests that traditions contribute to a sense of identity and belonging by connecting you to the people, experiences and shared values that have shaped your life. In fact, research focused on holiday rituals has found that participating in traditions such as preparing grandmother’s chocolate fudge or watching favorite seasonal movies is associated with greater feelings of closeness and enjoyment during celebrations.

You may not recognize how tightly some holiday traditions are tied to certain stages of your life. Parents who once looked forward to Christmas morning with young children may now find themselves coordinating celebrations around the schedules of adult children and their families and in-laws. Someone who has hosted holiday gatherings for decades may find themselves adjusting to being a guest rather than orchestrating the festivities.
Although these kinds of changes are a natural part of life, they can bring a mix of emotions. You can welcome new experiences while still missing aspects of an earlier time.
During these periods of transition, the memories associated with holiday traditions may become especially meaningful, offering a connection to the past as you adjust to the present.

If you find yourself missing the holidays of years past, you may be longing not for the celebration itself but for a particular era. Memories of former times can bring comfort, but they can also evoke feelings of grief, loneliness or sadness , particularly if you’re navigating changes you didn’t anticipate or would not have chosen, such as illness, injury, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People may be more inclined to experience nostalgia, a sentimental longing for the past , during periods of transition , when familiar aspects of life are changing.
While nostalgia is sometimes viewed negatively, as dwelling on past experiences, research suggests it can be a valuable resource when navigating life changes, especially for younger generations .

For instance, nostalgia can actually strengthen social connections and contribute to a sense of meaning. Recalling cherished memories can remind you you’re part of a broader life story, which can enhance feelings of connection, personal value and purpose.
Nostalgia can also help people make sense of the different chapters of life, allowing them to maintain a sense of who they are even as circumstances change.

Memories, then, can be more than reminders of what once was. They can help you recognize what you value and inform how you experience the present. While nostalgia may not ease the pain associated with challenges such as major health changes, evolving caregiving responsibilities or military deployment, it can serve as a bridge between the past and the present.

Throughout life, people adjust routines, responsibilities and expectations to accommodate new circumstances. Yet when it comes to the holidays, they may be reluctant to make those same adjustments. Is it still Thanksgiving if the table doesn’t feature the cranberry sauce made with your family’s traditional recipe? Can it feel like Christmas if there’s no tree decorated with your family’s sentimental ornaments?

This reluctance to let holiday observances evolve may be influenced, in part, by how people remember previous celebrations. Negative emotions associated with past experiences tend to fade more quickly than positive ones . You may remember the warmth of gathering around a holiday table but less readily recall the stress or challenges that accompanied it.

When expectations no longer reflect the realities of your life, you may feel disappointed or place pressure on yourself or others to live up to those old memories. Even a cherished tradition can become a source of stress when you feel obligated to maintain it in the same way year after year.

As you navigate life’s transitions, it may be helpful to reflect on what you cherish most about your holiday traditions. Is it the way you have always celebrated? Or is it the feelings of comfort and belonging that you associate with those celebrations?
Research suggests that reflecting on the past can inspire people to seek meaningful connections and experiences in the present .

Of course, adjusting to change is not always easy, and for some, the holidays can be particularly hard . Adapting does not mean abandoning cherished traditions, directly replacing what has been lost, or feeling pressured to create new memories. It may simply mean accepting that the holidays will feel different and allowing yourself the time and space to adjust.

In the desire to recreate what once was, many people may overlook the moments that could become cherished memories in the years ahead. Savor the memories of holidays past without expecting them to define how you experience the holidays today. Celebrations don’t need to remain the same to remain meaningful.

articles.title: Delridge Station bus loop
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Earlier this year Sound Transit provided a simplified design for the Delridge Link Station. If the West Seattle Link Extension gets built, Ross pointed out how RapidRide H buses will need to detour to serve the station. That would eliminate any travel time advantages gained by running on rails even if bus and trains would align their departure time perfectly. Instead of such detour, what about if the buses would just stop on Delridge Way and riders could take an overpass to the platform going north? It’s similar to RapidRide A buses stopping on International Blvd and riders taking an overpass to reach the airport station.
As most riders are expected to reach the station by bus, in particular RapidRide H, the transfer experience will be critical.

Early on Sound Transit had considered various designs for the Delridge Link station. Before settling on the location in front of the steel plant, one such design had been right above and along Delridge Way. Busses would have stopped right underneath, and riders could have just taken an escalator up to the departing platform. That would have provided a great transfer experience. With the current alignment and station location, designing a great transfer experience is more complicated. For southbound buses, Sound Transit plans a station along Delridge Way. For northbound buses, Sound Transit proposes that the buses detour from the red bus lane on the right to take a left turn into SW Andover St and a right turn into the station (see blue line on map below). But that also means buses have to pull out of the station and turn left again to get back to Delridge Way. Along the way they may need to navigate around the large trucks serving the steel plant. While riders get dropped off right under the Link platform, the various turns each bus has to navigate may add several minutes to the transfer.

If Sound Transit would instead add a northbound bus stop along Delridge Way across from the southbound bus stop and an overpass connecting to the northbound Link platform (see red lines on map), then riders could arrive quite quickly. (Southbound riders would need to take the escalator/elevator down and up again)

Sound Transit already plans a staircase on the NE corner of the station. Instead, they could build a staircase on the east side of Delridge Way and connect it with an overpass to the northbound platform. This would be similar to the way buses stop along the International Blvd to reach the airport station.

This would free up bus bays on the west side of the station. That space could be used as pickup/drop off and paratransit stop which may eliminate the need for the south car/van loop. That may allow larger housing developments on the south corner.

I am also concerned that the station entrance is quite a bit lower than Delridge Way. That may create some issues for riders who want to walk on the ground between buses along Delridge and the station. I really liked the plaza of the prior station design which allowed access to a mezzanine but understand that it adds cost. It would be great if the housing development could connect at least to the south staircases and elevators midway. If Sound Transit could add a small mezzanine under the tracks connecting the northbound and southbound southern staircases, it would help with at-grade walking to Delridge (and also switching platforms).

I still don’t think a Link extension to West Seattle is a good choice as buses could just drop riders off at SODO, but if we proceed with the plan, let’s at least optimize the existing design to improve the transfer experience as much as possible.

paras: Maybe it’s the wet and the gloom, maybe it’s the public transit system that slows to a crawl in the wee hours, or maybe it’s the fabled Seattle Freeze. Whatever the cause, our city’s late-night food scene is much-maligned, and there’s a grain of truth to this rep.

But if you know where to look, there are plenty of great places that stay open after 10 p.m., and even a handful after last call at 2 a.m. If there’s one thing we’ve learned in our relentless pursuit of a midnight (or much later) snack , it’s that the hours posted online are particularly unreliable for late-night spots. Instagram, a phone call, or word of mouth are typically your best bet for securing an after-hours bite. Well, that, and this list.
In our November 2026 update, we added Tacos Cometa, a Capitol Hill carne asada spot with fine dining pedigree, Jupiter Bar’s Good Shape Pizza, and reincarnated Seattle icon Bush Garden.

articles.title: Voters are fed up with for-profit utilities, but they keep rejecting ‘public power’
articles.author: Jesse Nichols
paras: Climate activists around the country saw this month’s midterm elections as a win. From congressional seats to governors’ mansions to local offices, progressive candidates leveraged voters’ frustration with the rising cost of living, especially high power bills, to defeat fossil fuel-friendly challengers.

But voters in two communities — Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Kitsap County, Washington — also rejected an idea that some say can address both climate change and affordability: replacing for-profit utilities with publicly owned ones.

On average, public utilities in the country charge lower electric rates and offer more reliable service than for-profit providers. Advocates contend that by being accountable to communities, they could transition to cleaner forms of energy faster than their counterparts beholden to shareholders and bottom lines.

Despite being in different regions of the country, the two community efforts unfolded in eerily similar ways. In each, private utilities spent roughly $2 million on local opposition campaigns, even using identical terms, like “too costly” and “too risky.” In the end, both initiatives failed, sharing the same fate as the vast majority of recent public power efforts around the country.

These results highlight the unique challenges of creating a new public power utility in the 21st century. A century ago, building a new public utility meant building a new grid. Today, it means buying out the poles and wires already owned by a for-profit utility, a process that more closely resembles a hostile takeover.

Public power has been an important part of Washington’s history for almost as long as Washington has been a state. But the movement really took off in the 1930s, triggered by two major events. First, a citizen-led state ballot initiative gave every community the right to form its own public utility district, or PUD. These new public agencies, run by elected commissioners, were empowered to provide power, water, and eventually internet to their constituents without taking a profit. Soon after, Congress created the Bonneville Power Administration, a New Deal-era agency that sold hydropower from the Columbia River. The new agency was required to give public utilities first dibs on its cheap hydropower, causing dozens of power districts to pop up around the state in the following decades.

It was in this golden age that Kitsap County — a community on the small peninsula across the Puget Sound from Seattle — formed its own public utility district intended to provide electricity. But the outbreak of World War II a few years later delayed that effort for long enough that its authorization expired. Today, the utility district oversees water and internet infrastructure but allows a private utility called Puget Sound Energy to provide power.

By the 1950s, the red-scare movement took aim at public power. Private utility groups ran ads in national magazines. “It was ‘creeping communism,’ and had pictures of Russian dictators,” said Steve Johnson, the former executive director of the Washington Public Utility Districts Association. Since then, public power has been in a dry spell, with most community efforts failing in Washington and across the U.S.

There was a notable exception in 2008, when Jefferson County — Kitsap’s rural neighbor to the west — passed a ballot initiative to create a new public utility that would take over power service from Puget Sound Energy. “I think that was a big wake-up call for the company, because there had not been a new PUD since the 1950s,” said Johnson. Today, Jefferson County runs entirely on carbon-free electricity from Bonneville Power, and typical bills there are roughly 19 percent lower than for Puget Sound Energy’s 1.24 million customers in surrounding areas.

Meanwhile, in neighboring Kitsap County, which today is home to about 280,000 people, Puget Sound Energy’s power rates continued to rise. Over the last five years, the average power bill has nearly doubled, and the company is proposing a series of increases totaling 32 percent by 2029. Puget Sound Energy told Grist that its rates reflect rising demand, infrastructure costs, and the challenge of meeting Washington’s clean electricity targets. State law requires utilities to be carbon neutral by 2030 , leaving Puget Sound Energy, which still gets about half its energy from fossil fuels, scrambling to meet deadlines.

Earlier this year, as bills with new rates arrived in mailboxes, Kitsap utility commissioners started to hear from residents struggling to make ends meet. “Not being able to decide between feeding your kids and paying your electric bill — it’s not OK,” said commissioner Heather Pauley. This led the utility district to put forward a ballot initiative asking voters to give it the authority to take over power service from Puget Sound Energy.

The initiative’s design had, in one commissioner’s words, an “Achilles’ heel.” Voters would be approving the proposal without an official feasibility study. If the measure passed, the district would pay for an extensive study on the plan’s costs and benefits. Only if it penciled out would the commissioners move ahead with taking over the grid. While this was intended as a gesture of fiscal responsibility, it also left voters with few details to vote on.

This ended up being the opening for Puget Sound Energy’s opposition campaign: “Too Costly. Too Risky. No Plan,” their flyers and yard signs read. The campaign spent $2.3 million, making it one of the most expensive local ballot measure fights in state history.

Meanwhile, the public utility district was strictly prohibited from any form of advocacy. “Was there misinformation out there? Absolutely,” said Angela Bennink, the district’s general manager. “But we were limited in what we could do.”

Unplug PSE, a grassroots campaign organized by Johnson and other Kitsap residents, took on the mantle of advocating for the initiative. But with a total budget of $9,000, they were thoroughly outmatched.

Puget Sound Energy also argued that a utility takeover would be too expensive — though much of that expense would come from the private utility itself. During Jefferson County’s buyout negotiations, Puget Sound Energy had demanded $109 million for all its power lines and transformers, more than double their assessed value. The private company was later ordered to return nearly $53 million of those extra proceeds back to its ratepayers. This time, Puget Sound Energy told Grist that it might not even agree to sell in the first place, meaning the public utility would have to pick an eminent domain fight.

With so many voters motivated by affordability concerns, the lack of financial details made the initiative a tough sell. “The ‘No Plan’ of that argument certainly sank in with a lot of people that we talked with,” said Fran Korten, chair of Unplug PSE. In the end, the proposition received only 42 percent approval from voters.

The utility district still has the authority to do a feasibility study, and could potentially make another try for public power in 2028. But Bennink thinks a critical window might be closing. Bonneville Power’s legacy dams and nuclear resources — the resources a theoretical Kitsap County public utility would rely on to provide affordable power to residents — are stretched pretty thin. The administration currently has enough cheap power to cover about 60 percent of the county’s electricity needs, Bennink said, but if another county set up a new public utility, it could claim that power first. This would mean the district could face many of the same market challenges as Puget Sound Energy, the private utility said.

As in much of the rest of the country, public power in Michigan was born out of necessity. For-profit utilities in the late 19th century had little incentive to serve small remote communities, so cities and towns across the Mitten State built their own power systems.
Today, the state has 41 municipally owned electric utilities in small and midsized cities. Almost all of them have been around for decades.

But two years ago, voters in Ann Arbor passed a ballot measure to create a municipal renewable power utility that residents could opt in to. It wouldn’t replace the city’s sole power utility, the for-profit company DTE Energy, but instead would pay for solar panels, batteries, and other infrastructure to feed into the existing grid. As of November, 92 homes in one neighborhood are participating in the pilot phase of the public utility, which aims to expand citywide next year.

But some said this plan didn’t go far enough. The dual-utility model still hinges on DTE’s aging infrastructure, and an analysis by the city indicates that the for-profit utility won’t add renewable energy fast enough to help Ann Arbor reach its 100 percent renewable energy goal by the end of the decade.

So public power advocates in Ann Arbor last year decided to go a step further and push for cutting out DTE, which would allow the city to transition to clean energy faster. They put a proposal on the ballot this year to ask voters whether Ann Arbor should establish a board to lead a transition away from DTE, with the goal of completely replacing the for-profit utility with a brand-new one that’s owned and operated by the city.

“We could make electricity more affordable for people in Ann Arbor. We could make it more reliable,” said Fiona Dunlop, a field organizer for the group Ann Arbor for Public Power, which wrote and advocated for the ballot proposal. “We could take real steps toward good climate policies.”

Supporters of the ballot measure were up against fierce opposition from DTE, labor unions and even the city itself . “The complexity of our proposal made it easier for our opponents to find inroads to attack,” said Brian Geiringer, the executive director of Ann Arbor for Public Power. DTE poured $1.8 million into a group called the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition, which campaigned against the proposal.

Using the same words as Puget Sound Energy, it argued that movement toward public power would be “too costly and too risky” for Ann Arbor and its roughly 125,000 residents. A board could be made up of people with little to no technical experience and ultimately leave residents with higher costs, the coalition said.

“The people of Ann Arbor saw this proposal for exactly what it was: a mandate that would have made life in Ann Arbor even more expensive by eventually forcing working families to carry the burden of a billion-dollar debt,” the coalition said in a statement after the election, referencing the cost of buying out and maintaining the infrastructure. The $1 billion refers to the coalition’s estimate of how much it would cost the city to buy DTE’s poles and wires, plus how much to maintain that infrastructure. The city estimated in a 2023 early-phase feasibility study that a buyout could cost anywhere from $281 million to $1.15 billion, noting that there’s no modern precedent in Michigan to point to. It could be paid for by issuing bonds, but further financing options would require another feasibility study.
Ultimately, the ballot proposal failed by a slim margin of 3.6 percent, or 2,003 votes.

Like the rest of the country, Ann Arbor residents are frustrated with rising power bills and unreliable service, said Mike Shriberg, a professor of practice and engagement at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability. But the high, uncertain costs of public power might have edged out these concerns, for now. And as in Kitsap County, voters did not have a full feasibility study to consider.
“I don’t think it was actually a debate about the fundamentals of whether public power would be a good thing here in concept,” Shriberg said. “It was really about the details.”

The challenge of creating a new electric utility in the 21st century is “fundamentally different” than it was in the 1930s, Bennink said. A century ago, the power grid was in its infancy, and public utilities were largely building networks from the ground up. Today, creating a public utility instead involves billion-dollar buyouts, well-funded opposition campaigns, and uphill battles with powerful private companies that have every incentive to not cooperate. “It would have been very, very hard,” Bennink said. “Herculean. Monumental.”

Despite the challenges, some say interest in public power will likely keep growing across the country as frustration with utilities continues to mount. “As we’ve seen across the country, there’s an incredible amount of pent-up frustration with our electric utilities,” said Shriberg at the University of Michigan. “Costs are too high, the service is too unreliable and too dirty.”

The lack of details may have been the downfall for the public power ballot questions in Washington and Michigan. But there are signs that government leaders are willing to consider the option if there’s more planning involved. The City Council in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, voted unanimously this month to fund a $1.35 million feasibility study to explore replacing investor-owned We Energies with a city utility. The decision came after the state’s public service commission approved a rate increase for We Energies.

In Kitsap County, many public power supporters are now pushing for a similar plan. At a post-election utility district meeting, the small conference room was unusually packed with residents asking commissioners to perform a feasibility study.

Election Day was “bittersweet” for Ann Arbor organizers going up against utilities. While the public power proposal failed locally, an ambitious statewide ballot measure that would amend Michigan campaign finance laws to rein in utilities’ influence in elections overwhelmingly passed — including among Ann Arbor voters. And public power supporters still see opportunities to move the needle on a grid takeover: The newly elected mayor of Ann Arbor endorsed the public power ballot measure during his campaign, and the City Council saw turnover that could result in a new look at funding for a deeper feasibility study, which failed to pass last year .
“The movement is still very much alive, probably stronger than ever,” Geiringer said.
Correction: This story originally mischaracterized the margins by which both ballot measured failed and misstated the name of the Washington Public Utility Districts Association.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of October 2026: tamale and specialty coffee haven Cafetal Quilombo Cafe, Thai dumpling hotspot E-Jae Pak Mor, and Dim Sum King, which reigns supreme in counter-service dim sum.

A note on pricing: $ means entrees are mostly under $15; $$ means entrees are mostly under $25; $$$ means entrees are priced under $35; and $$$$ means entrees are more expensive than that, or it is primarily a tasting menu restaurant. (Prices are always subject to change.)
